claims.text: In FeNiCrCoMn, retention of toughness under demanding conditions is governed by the extent and morphology of short-range chemical ordering.
Controlled heat treatment can change the degree or morphology of short-range order.
A homogenized FeNiCrCoMn state has minimal or diminished short-range order.
Enhanced short-range order promotes the formation of nanoscale crack-bridging structures in FeNiCrCoMn.
Nanoscale crack bridges form near crack tips in CrMnFeCoNi.
Near-tip nanoscale crack bridges shield the crack tip and impede or delay crack propagation.
Short-range ordering produces local chemical or compositional heterogeneity.
Short-range-order-induced changes in dislocation slip deflect crack propagation in FeNiCrCoMn.
Short-range-order-induced chemical heterogeneity supports nucleation of nanoscale crack bridges.
Nanoscale crack bridges provide extrinsic toughening.
A homogenized FeNiCrCoMn microstructure lacks nanoscale crack-bridging features.
A homogenized FeNiCrCoMn microstructure has lower intrinsic resistance to fracture.
Heat treatments that enhance short-range order will increase the frequency or extent of nanoscale crack bridges relative to a homogenized baseline.
Heat treatments that enhance short-range order will alter crack-tip dislocation patterns relative to a homogenized baseline.
Heat treatments that enhance short-range order will measurably increase FeNiCrCoMn fracture toughness relative to a homogenized baseline.
The proposed relationship is limited to processing conditions that do not induce secondary-phase separation or other phase transformations.
The magnitude of any toughness improvement and the evolution of crack-tip microstructure remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis correctly describes crack bridging as an extrinsic shielding mechanism but then says that absence of bridges reduces intrinsic fracture resistance. Removing an extrinsic mechanism can reduce measured toughness, but it does not by itself establish reduced intrinsic fracture resistance.
